sources.entry: Hoard: A Scalable Memory Allocator for Multithreaded Applications - Defines blowup and allocator-induced false sharing, which per-processor heaps under a bounded global heap avoid.

summary.title: Hoard: A Scalable Memory Allocator for Multithreaded Applications
summary.one_liner: Learn how Hoard's per-processor heaps, a bounded global heap, and superblock transfers keep multithreaded malloc/free scalable while limiting blowup and allocator-induced false sharing.
keywords: how to avoid false sharing in malloc
why does malloc slow down on multiple cores
takeaways: Blowup is memory consumption growth from a concurrent allocator failing to reuse freed memory; producer-consumer patterns can trigger it, from a factor of P up to unbounded.
Allocator-induced false sharing happens actively when one cache line is split among threads' allocations, and passively when frees let threads reuse pieces of shared lines.
Hoard uses per-processor heaps plus one global heap; superblocks move to the global heap when a per-processor heap becomes more than f empty, bounding blowup to a constant factor.
Each superblock is owned by one heap at a time, so simultaneous allocations come from different superblocks, and frees return blocks to their superblock, avoiding most false sharing.
The paper reports Hoard improving on the Solaris allocator by up to 60x on 14 processors and up to 18x over the next best allocator tested.
summary.summary: The paper introduces Hoard, a multithreaded memory allocator for C and C++ programs that aims for speed, scalability, false sharing avoidance, and low fragmentation. It defines blowup and explains how both active and passive allocator-induced false sharing arise. Hoard combines per-processor heaps with a global heap and manages fixed-size superblocks, transferring a superblock to the global heap when a per-processor heap crosses an emptiness threshold. The authors sketch proofs bounding blowup and synchronization costs, and report empirical results on eleven programs against serial and concurrent allocators.
